title: Sarah Imperiled, the Promise Preserved
summary: On the eve of Isaac’s birth Abraham repeats his half-truth in Gerar, and God protects Sarah, rebukes the deceiver through a pagan king, and heals through intercession.
historicalContext: After the overthrow of Sodom, Abraham leaves the oaks of Mamre and moves into the Negeb, the dry southern fringe of Canaan, pasturing between the oasis of Kadesh and the frontier wall of Shur before staying near Gerar, a fertile town between Gaza and Beersheba. He is a resident alien, without clan protection or legal standing among settled city-states. Royal harems in that world often absorbed women from prominent households, and a marriage with the family of a wealthy chieftain could seal an alliance. The narrative also assumes a moral order known well before Sinai: adultery was recognized across the ancient Near East as a “great sin,” and a king could speak of conscience, guilt, and restitution. Sarah is about ninety, the conception of Isaac has been promised within the year, and the household of Abimelech is the setting in which that promise is suddenly placed at risk.
literaryContext: Genesis 20 is the second of three wife-sister episodes (12:10–20; 26:1–11), and its wording assumes the reader remembers Egypt. It stands between the destruction of Sodom and the birth of Isaac, so that the promised seed is endangered at the last possible moment. The chapter is built almost wholly from dialogue: God and Abimelech in the night, Abimelech and his servants at dawn, Abimelech and Abraham in open court, and the king’s closing words to Abraham and Sarah. The phrase “Sarah his wife” and its equivalents frame and run through the account, keeping the marriage at the center. Ironies accumulate: the pagan king pleads for righteousness as Abraham had pleaded for Sodom, the man who feared there was no fear of God is himself rebuked by a God-fearing ruler, and the barren Sarah’s husband prays open the wombs of Gerar just before her own is opened in chapter 21.
themes: God’s faithfulness preserving the promised seed
Fear of man and the half-truth that deceives
The sanctity of marriage before Sinai
The flawed prophet as intercessor for the nations
Life and fruitfulness in the hand of God

outline.title: Sarah Taken in Gerar
outline.summary: Abraham sojourns in Gerar, calls Sarah his sister again, and Abimelech brings her into his household.

outline.title: God Confronts the King by Night
outline.summary: God warns Abimelech of death, acknowledges his integrity, explains that he restrained him, and commands Sarah’s return through the prophet’s prayer.

outline.title: The Pagan King Rebukes the Prophet
outline.summary: Abimelech’s court fears God, and the king demands an account from Abraham, who pleads fear, a technical truth, and a long-standing arrangement.

outline.title: Restitution and Public Vindication
outline.summary: Abimelech restores Sarah with gifts, offers Abraham the land, and gives a large sum that clears Sarah’s honor before all.

outline.title: Intercession and Healing
outline.summary: Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s household and opens the wombs he had closed because of Sarah.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham journeyed from thence toward the south country, and dwelled between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“From thence” points back to the oaks of Mamre near Hebron, where Abraham had received the three visitors and pleaded for Sodom (18:1, 22–33). The narrative gives no reason for the move. Fresh pasture for large flocks is a natural explanation, and the ruined plain to the east may have made the region unsettled, yet Scripture leaves the motive unstated. What it records is the direction: “toward the south country,” the Negeb, the same direction Abraham had taken before the famine drove him into Egypt (12:9–10). The echo is deliberate. The reader who remembers that earlier journey senses trouble before a word of dialogue is spoken.

Kadesh was an oasis deep in the southern wilderness, and Shur lay near the Egyptian frontier, the region where the angel had once met Hagar beside a spring (16:7, 14). This was dry grazing land. Gerar lay further north, in a well-watered valley between Gaza and Beersheba, a royal town with fields and wells. Abraham “dwelled” in the broad region and “sojourned” in Gerar, and the Hebrew plays on the sound of the verb and the city’s name. He comes as a resident alien, a guest without rights of citizenship.

That status matters theologically. Lot had moved from Zoar to a mountain cave and then fades from the story; Abraham keeps moving as a stranger in the land God had promised him. Hebrews reads that pilgrim life as faith that looked for “a city which hath foundations” (Hebrews 11:9–10). Yet the same openness to a new place carries risk. The pilgrim who has no clan to defend him may be tempted to defend himself, and that is exactly what follows.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּגָר בִּגְרָר (wayyagor bigrar) — and sojourned in Gerar
wordNotes.explanation: The verb גּוּר (gur) means to live as a resident alien, a person dwelling among a people without belonging to them by birth. The related noun גֵּר (ger) later describes the stranger whom Israel must protect, because Israel too had been strangers in Egypt. The sound play with the town’s name ties Abraham’s identity as a sojourner to the place itself, and the same verb closes the Gerar episodes when he sojourns “many days” in the Philistines’ land.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister: and Abimelech king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verse is startling in its brevity. With no description of fear, no conversation with Sarah, and no famine to explain it, Abraham simply says, “She is my sister.” Verse 13 will reveal that this had been a standing arrangement since the couple first left Haran, so the words are a habit rather than a sudden impulse. That makes them more troubling. The man who had defeated four eastern kings with his trained servants (14:14–16), who had heard the covenant promises repeated and confirmed, and who had stood before the LORD interceding for Sodom now falls back on an old ruse before the ruler of a single town. About twenty-five years had passed since Egypt, and the lesson of that humiliation had evidently faded.

The timing makes the lapse grave. In chapter 17 God had named Sarah as the mother of the covenant son, and in chapter 18 He had fixed the time: “at the time appointed I will return unto thee… and Sarah shall have a son” (18:14). Abraham now exposes the very woman through whom the promise is to come. Behind the human weakness stands the older conflict announced in Eden, where enmity was set between the serpent and the woman’s seed (3:15). Again and again in Genesis the line of promise is threatened just before a birth, and each time God alone preserves it.

Abimelech “sent, and took Sarah.” The name means “my father is king” and seems to have served as a royal title at Gerar, since a later king in Isaac’s day bears it as well (26:1). Sarah was about ninety. Whether the king was drawn by her beauty, by the political value of a marriage tie with a rich and powerful chieftain, or by both, the text does not say. What it stresses is the repeated phrase “Sarah his wife.” The narrator never lets the reader forget whose wife she is, even when Abraham does.

wordNotes.term: אֲחֹתִי הִוא (ʾaḥoti hiwʾ) — she is my sister
wordNotes.explanation: The same two words appear in Egypt and again on Isaac’s lips in Gerar. Abraham can claim a literal basis, since Sarah was his half sister, yet he used the phrase to conceal the marriage and invite a false conclusion. Scripture treats such speech as deception, whatever technical accuracy it may contain.

verses.bibleText: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him, Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But God came.” The adversative turns the story. Abraham has been silent before God and spoken only to men, and now God takes the initiative toward a man outside the covenant. The narrator uses Elohim, the general name for God, through most of the chapter, the name suited to dealings with the nations, until the covenant name returns in verse 18. God speaks in “a dream by night,” the mode of revelation He uses with Laban, with Pharaoh in Joseph’s day, and with Nebuchadnezzar. Here the dream needs no interpreter; it is plain speech, as direct as a court sentence.

The sentence is blunt: “Behold, thou art but a dead man.” The Hebrew is a participial clause, “behold, you are dying,” describing death as imminent and already at work. Verse 17 suggests that a malady had already struck the royal household, and the closing of wombs shows that God’s hand was present before the king understood why. The ground of the sentence is stated twice: “for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man’s wife.” No law code had yet been given at Sinai, and Abimelech needs no explanation of why taking another man’s wife is a capital wrong. Marriage as God instituted it in Eden binds one man and one woman (2:24), and the seventh commandment later puts in writing what conscience already knew.

The severity serves mercy. God warns before He strikes, opening a way of life to the king, and in doing so He protects Sarah, guards the marriage, and keeps the promised son’s parentage beyond doubt. Death here is the real wage of sin, the same sentence pronounced in Eden, and the same voice that pronounces it will name the way to escape it.

wordNotes.term: הִנְּךָ מֵת (hinneka met) — behold, thou art but a dead man
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “behold, you are dying.” The participle מֵת (met) presents death as impending, with הִנֵּה (hinneh) calling urgent attention to it. The phrase marks a sentence already in force unless something changes, which verse 7 then supplies.

wordNotes.term: בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל (beʿulat baʿal) — a man’s wife
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means a woman married to a husband, using a verb and noun from the same stem for emphasis. It appears in the law forbidding adultery with a married woman, which treated the offense as capital. Genesis shows the principle already recognized before that law was written.

verses.bibleText: But Abimelech had not come near her: and he said, Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator first establishes the decisive fact: “Abimelech had not come near her.” The verb qarab, “come near,” is the idiom Leviticus uses for sexual relations, so the statement clears the king of adultery and, with it, removes any question about the parentage of the son Sarah will soon bear. Isaac’s birth in chapter 21 must be beyond suspicion, and the narrative closes that door before the dialogue begins.

Abimelech answers the dream with a question: “Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?” He addresses God as ʾAdonai, a title of respect, and appeals to divine justice. The wording recalls Abraham’s own intercession only two chapters earlier: “Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?” (18:23). Now a Philistine king pleads the very principle Abraham had pressed for Sodom, and he does so on behalf of a people who, in this matter, have done nothing wrong. The irony is pointed. The man of promise has no part in this conversation, while an outsider argues that the Judge of all the earth must do right.

The king speaks of his “nation” because ruler and people stood together before God; his guilt would fall on all his house. His appeal does not deny that adultery deserves death; it denies that he has knowingly committed it.

wordNotes.term: הֲגוֹי גַּם־צַדִּיק (hagoy gam-tsaddiq) — a righteous nation also
wordNotes.explanation: צַדִּיק (tsaddiq) here means innocent in the matter at hand, not sinless in every respect. The question echoes Abraham’s plea for the righteous in Sodom, and the word גּוֹי (goy), nation, is the same term used in the promise that Abraham would become a great nation.

verses.bibleText: Said he not unto me, She is my sister? and she, even she herself said, He is my brother: in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands have I done this.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech lays out his defense with the clarity of a witness in court. Abraham said, “She is my sister,” and Sarah, “even she herself,” confirmed it with “He is my brother.” The repetition places the deception on both of them. Sarah had not been a passive pawn in this arrangement; she had spoken the agreed words. The king acted on the testimony of the only two people who knew the truth.

His claim of innocence pairs the inner and outer life: “in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands.” Heart and hands together describe motive and action. The same pairing appears in the psalm that asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and answers, “He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:4). Abimelech had no covenant, no altar of Abraham’s God, and no written law, yet conscience bore witness within him, the very thing Paul describes among nations that do by nature what the law requires (Romans 2:14–15). His protest is honest, and God will not dispute it.

wordNotes.term: בְּתָם־לְבָבִי וּבְנִקְיֹן כַּפַּי (betom-levavi uvniqyon kappay) — in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands
wordNotes.explanation: תֹּם (tom) denotes wholeness or blamelessness, the quality ascribed to Job and to David’s heart; נִקָּיוֹן (niqqayon) means cleanness or freedom from guilt. Together they claim upright motive and uncompromised action in this specific matter.

verses.bibleText: And God said unto him in a dream, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God answers the king again “in a dream,” and His first word is agreement: “Yea, I know.” The emphatic pronoun in Hebrew stresses that God Himself has full knowledge of the heart. Abimelech’s plea is accepted. He had acted in the integrity of his heart, and the Judge who searches hearts says so openly. Yet God adds what the king could not have known: “for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.”

The sentence shifts the credit. Abimelech’s clean record was real, but it was not his achievement alone. God had restrained him, apparently through the illness hinted at in verse 17, so that his good intention never had opportunity to become a grievous act in ignorance. A clear conscience is precious; it is never a self-made shield. Divine providence had stood between the king and the deed, as it stands between countless people and the sins they would otherwise fall into. David later prayed, “Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins” (Psalm 19:13), recognizing that preservation from sin is itself a gift of grace.

The phrase “sinning against me” is equally significant. Taking another man’s wife would wrong Abraham and Sarah, but God names Himself as the One offended. Joseph will later say the same when tempted in Potiphar’s house: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” (39:9). David confesses, “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). Every breach of marriage is first a breach against its Author, who joined man and woman in Eden and whose law guards that union. The moral order here operates long before Sinai; God holds a Philistine king accountable for a commandment He would later write in stone.

There is a further mercy for Sarah. She had been placed in danger by her husband’s fear and her own complicity, and no human being was positioned to defend her. God was. He kept her untouched, preserved the integrity of her marriage, and safeguarded the son to be born of it.

wordNotes.term: וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ (waʾeḥsokh) — and I withheld
wordNotes.explanation: The verb חָשַׂךְ (ḥasakh) means to hold back or restrain. It describes Abraham not withholding Isaac on Moriah, and David being kept back from bloodshed by Abigail’s intervention. Here God is the One who restrains, keeping Abimelech from an act he would otherwise have committed.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live: and if thou restore her not, know thou that thou shalt surely die, thou, and all that are thine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Acknowledgment of innocence does not end the matter. God gives a command with a promise and a warning: “Now therefore restore the man his wife… and thou shalt live: and if thou restore her not, know thou that thou shalt surely die, thou, and all that are thine.” Abimelech has done no conscious wrong, yet a wrong situation exists, and it must be put right. Sarah must go home. Integrity of heart does not cancel the obligation to repair harm once its true nature is known. Later Israel would learn the same principle through offerings for sins committed in ignorance, which still required acknowledgment and restoration (Leviticus 5:17–18).

Then comes a surprising description of the man who caused the trouble: “for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee.” This is the first time the word naviʾ appears in Scripture. Abraham has not delivered any message to Abimelech, and his recent words have been anything but prophetic. God calls him a prophet because of his standing with God, the one who has received God’s word and may speak to God on behalf of others. In the patriarchal setting, the prophet is a man admitted to God’s counsel; the LORD had said, “Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?” (18:17). The Psalms later recall this very episode: “Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm” (Psalm 105:15).

The arrangement is humbling for both men. Abimelech, the innocent party, must seek the prayer of the guilty one. Abraham, who has endangered the king’s life, must now intercede for the life of the man he wronged. God does not choose His channel of blessing by comparing the moral records of two men in a single episode. He works through the covenant He has made, so that the promise “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (12:3) finds a small fulfillment even in the aftermath of Abraham’s failure. Grace, not merit, keeps the promise moving.

The warning “thou shalt surely die” repeats the doubled form God used in Eden (2:17). Life and death hang on response to God’s word. Abraham’s role as intercessor anticipates the long line of prophets who prayed for others—Moses for Miriam and for Israel, Samuel for the people, Job for his friends—and ultimately points to the One who “ever liveth to make intercession” for those who come to God by Him (Hebrews 7:25). Unlike Abraham, that Intercessor has no failure of His own to answer for, and His plea on our behalf never falters.

wordNotes.term: נָבִיא (naviʾ) — prophet
wordNotes.explanation: The first biblical occurrence of the word. It most likely means one called by God to speak for Him, and the role includes standing before God for others. The Septuagint renders it προφήτης (prophētēs), one who speaks on behalf of another. Abraham is so named here in connection with intercession rather than prediction, showing that prayer for others belongs to the prophetic office.

wordNotes.term: וְיִתְפַּלֵּל בַּעַדְךָ (weyitpallel baʿadeka) — and he shall pray for thee
wordNotes.explanation: The verb פָּלַל (palal) in this reflexive form is the common word for prayer, often prayer that intercedes. With בַּעַד (baʿad), on behalf of, it describes standing before God for another person, as Moses did for Israel and Samuel for the nation.

verses.bibleText: Therefore Abimelech rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears: and the men were sore afraid.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech does not wait. He “rose early in the morning,” the phrase Genesis uses for prompt obedience, as when Abraham rises early to send Hagar away and again to journey to Moriah (21:14; 22:3). The king gathers “all his servants,” a term that includes his officials and court, and tells “all these things in their ears.” Nothing is concealed. The ruler who had innocently endangered his people now brings them into the knowledge of what God had said.

Their response is fear: “the men were sore afraid.” This is the fear of God that Abraham was sure would not be found in Gerar (v. 11). It sits at the center of the chapter, and it rebukes the man of faith before Abimelech ever opens his mouth to question him. People whom Abraham had written off as godless take God’s warning with utmost seriousness, much as the sailors and Ninevites of Jonah’s day would tremble at a word the prophet himself was reluctant to honor.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּירְאוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים מְאֹד (wayyireʾu haʾanashim meʾod) — and the men were sore afraid
wordNotes.explanation: The verb יָרֵא (yareʾ), to fear, is the root of the noun Abraham uses in verse 11, “the fear of God.” The narrator uses the same word for the court’s reaction, answering in advance Abraham’s assumption before he states it.

verses.bibleText: Then Abimelech called Abraham, and said unto him, What hast thou done unto us? and what have I offended thee, that thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin? thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having been cleared by God, Abimelech summons Abraham and confronts him with three questions and a verdict. “What hast thou done unto us?” The plural is significant: the king thinks of his people, not only himself. “What have I offended thee?” He asks whether he had wronged Abraham in some way that would explain such treatment. “That thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin?” The deception had placed a whole nation under the threat of judgment. Then the verdict: “thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done.”

“A great sin” is a term for adultery in other ancient documents, and in Scripture it later describes Israel’s spiritual adultery with the golden calf (Exodus 32:21, 30–31). The king understands that, even unknowingly, he had come to the brink of an offense that God treats with the utmost seriousness. Sin, in this narrative, is not only a matter of intention; a situation can carry guilt that must be dealt with even when the person involved acted in ignorance.

The scene reverses the expected roles. Abraham had been chosen to bring the knowledge of God to the nations, yet here a king of the nations instructs Abraham in elementary morality. Pharaoh had rebuked him in Egypt; now a second ruler does the same, and more fully. The reproach is just, and Abraham has no answer to it. Scripture does not shield its heroes from such moments. When believers act out of fear rather than faith, they can bring reproach on the name they bear and harm on those who trusted them (Romans 2:24).

wordNotes.term: חֲטָאָה גְדֹלָה (ḥataʾah gedolah) — a great sin
wordNotes.explanation: The noun derives from חָטָא (ḥataʾ), to miss the mark or sin. With “great,” the phrase describes adultery here and idolatry at Sinai, two kinds of covenant unfaithfulness Scripture often pairs. Abimelech uses it to show that the offense would have touched his entire kingdom.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said unto Abraham, What sawest thou, that thou hast done this thing?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A fresh introduction, “And Abimelech said,” suggests a pause in which Abraham gave no reply, so the king presses again: “What sawest thou, that thou hast done this thing?” The question asks what Abraham had observed in Gerar that could justify such distrust. Had the king or his people given some sign of violence or lawlessness? The question is fair and searching, and it allows Abraham to explain himself, which a harsher ruler might not have done.

The question exposes the real problem. Abraham had seen nothing. His fear rested on assumption rather than evidence, and the plan he had made years before had been applied by habit to a people he had not troubled to know. Prejudgment of this kind feels like prudence to the one who practices it. Scripture names it otherwise: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Proverbs 18:13), and Jesus warns against judging “according to the appearance” (John 7:24). Abraham had answered before he heard.

wordNotes.term: מָה רָאִיתָ (mah raʾita) — what sawest thou
wordNotes.explanation: The verb רָאָה (raʾah), to see, can mean to perceive or to have in view. Abimelech asks what Abraham had observed or intended, inviting an account of motives. The answer in verse 11 shows that Abraham’s judgment came from imagined danger rather than anything seen.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said, Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham’s reply begins with an admission: “Because I thought.” Literally, “I said,” meaning he had told himself. His reasoning ran in two steps: “Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife’s sake.” He had judged Gerar by its foreignness and concluded that a people without the true God would stop at nothing to take a beautiful woman. Fresh from the destruction of Sodom, where the absence of the fear of God had indeed been total, he may have assumed every Canaanite town was the same.

The narrative has already shown how mistaken he was. Abimelech had pleaded justice before God, acknowledged the sanctity of marriage, obeyed immediately, and assembled a court that trembled at God’s word. The fear of God was present in Gerar. What was missing in that moment was the fear of God in Abraham. Had he feared God rightly, he would not have feared men so much. “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Proverbs 29:25). The snare had closed on Abraham, and on Abimelech too, because the man of faith trusted his own scheme more than the One who had promised to be his shield (15:1).

The phrase “fear of God” in this context refers to a basic reverence for God that restrains wrongdoing and respects moral boundaries. Joseph will use it to reassure his brothers: “This do, and live; for I fear God” (42:18). Midwives in Egypt will show it by refusing Pharaoh’s order (Exodus 1:17). It is the moral awareness the Creator has placed in human conscience, and Abraham should not have assumed its absence. His error carries a warning for every believer who stands among unbelievers. It is easy to presume the worst about others, to treat them as beyond the reach of conscience, and to act defensively in ways that betray our own faith. God’s people may find, as Abraham did, that those they distrusted are more honest than they themselves have been.

wordNotes.term: יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים (yirʾat ʾelohim) — the fear of God
wordNotes.explanation: This expression describes reverence for God that shows itself in moral restraint, especially toward the vulnerable. It is used of those outside Israel as well as within, and its absence marks Amalek’s cruelty toward stragglers. Abraham assumed that Gerar lacked it, but the narrative proves him wrong.

wordNotes.term: רַק (raq) — surely
wordNotes.explanation: The particle usually means only or nothing but. Abraham’s statement is literally “there is just no fear of God in this place,” a sweeping and absolute judgment. The word exposes how far his fear had generalized from a single assumption.

verses.bibleText: And yet indeed she is my sister; she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham now offers a defense on the facts: “And yet indeed she is my sister; she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother.” This explains a detail Genesis had not given before. Sarah was Terah’s daughter by another wife, making her Abraham’s half sister. Such marriages were permitted in the patriarchal age; the later law forbidding marriage with a half sister came with Israel’s covenant at Sinai (Leviticus 18:9). Abraham’s statement was true as far as it went.

The problem lies in how far it went. “And she became my wife” is the fact that mattered, and it is the fact Abraham had concealed. Speech that selects true details in order to create a false belief is deception, whatever the literal accuracy of each word. The ninth commandment forbids false witness, and its scope covers misleading testimony that harms a neighbor. Abraham’s half-truth had nearly cost Abimelech his life and Sarah her honor.

Scripture’s standard is clear: “Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3:9). The language of Jesus is simpler still: “Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Matthew 5:37). Abraham’s defense did not convince Abimelech, and it does not satisfy the narrator, who never calls Sarah anything but Abraham’s wife.

wordNotes.term: וְגַם־אָמְנָה (wegam-ʾomnah) — and yet indeed
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb אָמְנָה (ʾomnah), truly or in fact, comes from the same family as אָמֵן (ʾamen). Abraham uses it to insist on the factual accuracy of his claim, though the claim was employed to mislead. Outside this verse it appears only in Achan’s confession of his sin at Ai.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when God caused me to wander from my father's house, that I said unto her, This is thy kindness which thou shalt shew unto me; at every place whither we shall come, say of me, He is my brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham completes his defense by revealing that the sister claim had been a settled policy: “at every place whither we shall come, say of me, He is my brother.” The arrangement went back to the beginning of his journeys, “when God caused me to wander from my father’s house.” What had happened in Egypt had not been a single lapse under famine pressure but one application of a plan agreed before the couple ever entered Canaan. Years without serious trouble may have made it seem harmless. “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecclesiastes 8:11).

The way Abraham describes his calling is telling. God had said, “Get thee out of thy country… unto a land that I will shew thee” (12:1), a summons full of promise. Speaking to a pagan king, Abraham describes it as being made to wander, using a verb that elsewhere describes straying or staggering, and the verb is plural in form, which a Philistine hearer could easily take as “the gods caused me to wander.” Whatever Abraham intended, he missed the moment to testify plainly to the God who had guided and blessed him for a quarter of a century. Fear had flattened his witness into the language of a homeless drifter.

He also calls the arrangement Sarah’s “kindness” to him, using the word ḥesed, the loyal love that binds covenant partners. Abraham asked his wife to show loyalty by concealing their marriage, so that the language of covenant faithfulness was bent to serve self-protection. The phrase is painful to read. Sarah’s safety and honor were the price of his own security. True ḥesed would have moved the husband to protect the wife; here the wife is asked to shield the husband at her own risk.

wordNotes.term: הִתְעוּ (hitʿu) — caused me to wander
wordNotes.explanation: The verb תָּעָה (taʿah) means to wander, go astray, or stagger, and is often used of sheep or of people led into error. With the plural form after Elohim, the expression is ambiguous, perhaps deliberately so when spoken to a pagan. It is a strikingly bleak description of a call that Genesis presents as purposeful.

wordNotes.term: חַסְדֵּךְ (ḥasdek) — thy kindness
wordNotes.explanation: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) denotes steadfast, loyal love within a relationship of commitment, the quality God shows to His covenant people. Abraham applies it to Sarah’s compliance with the sister scheme, turning a word of faithful devotion into a request for concealment.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants, and gave them unto Abraham, and restored him Sarah his wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech’s actions answer Abraham’s excuses more eloquently than any argument. He gives “sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants,” and he “restored him Sarah his wife.” The list recalls Pharaoh’s gifts in Egypt (12:16), but the circumstances differ. Pharaoh had given gifts when he took Sarah, as a kind of bride payment; Abimelech gives them when he returns her, as a public sign that he means no wrong and seeks peace with Abraham and his God.

The narrator again calls Sarah “his wife.” Her marital status had never changed while she was in the king’s household, and now it is openly acknowledged. Sarah returns untouched, ready to bear the son of promise as Abraham’s wife.

There is grace, too, in the abundance. Abraham, who had acted in fear, comes away from the episode richer than before. This does not mean that God rewarded his deception. The blessing flowed from God’s commitment to the covenant and from Abimelech’s desire to make things right with a man whom God called a prophet. The undeserved prosperity is a further rebuke, since Abraham had feared loss and received gifts.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּשֶׁב (wayyasheb) — and restored
wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of שׁוּב (shub), to return, means to bring back or give back. It answers God’s command in verse 7, “restore the man his wife,” using the same verb, and shows Abimelech’s exact obedience.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said, Behold, my land is before thee: dwell where it pleaseth thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The king’s next words offer what Pharaoh had refused: “Behold, my land is before thee: dwell where it pleaseth thee.” Pharaoh had said, in effect, take her and go (12:19); Abimelech invites Abraham to stay. The gift of residence goes beyond compensation. It expresses trust and a desire for continuing peace with a household where God is evidently present, a relationship that will be formalized by covenant at Beersheba in the next chapter (21:22–32).

The offer also carries a hint of the larger promise. God had pledged the land to Abraham’s descendants, and here a ruler of the land freely grants him room to live in it. The language recalls Abraham’s own generosity toward Lot, “Is not the whole land before thee?” (13:9). The land will not be seized through Abraham’s own schemes; it will be received as gift, as God intended from the start, and Abraham’s heirs will learn to say that the earth is the LORD’s to give.

wordNotes.term: בַּטּוֹב בְּעֵינֶיךָ שֵׁב (baṭṭov beʿeneka shev) — dwell where it pleaseth thee
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in what is good in your eyes, dwell.” The idiom grants full freedom of choice. The verb יָשַׁב (yashab), to settle or dwell, signals permanent residence rather than a passing stay, a step beyond the sojourning of verse 1.

verses.bibleText: And unto Sarah he said, Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver: behold, he is to thee a covering of the eyes, unto all that are with thee, and with all other: thus she was reproved.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abimelech now turns to Sarah, the person most wronged, and speaks to her directly: “Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver.” The word “pieces” is supplied; the unit is almost certainly the shekel, a weight of silver rather than a coin, since coinage did not yet exist. A thousand shekels would weigh roughly twenty-five pounds, a vast sum in a world where a laborer might earn a fraction of a shekel a month. It dwarfs the four hundred shekels Abraham would later pay for the cave of Machpelah (23:15–16). The size of the gift matches the gravity of the offense the king had nearly committed.

The phrase “thy brother” may carry a touch of irony. Abimelech now knows Abraham is Sarah’s husband, and his choice of the word the couple had used may gently expose the pretense. He pays through Abraham, as was fitting when honoring a married woman, but he names Sarah as the one for whose sake it is given.

“He is to thee a covering of the eyes” is the hardest phrase in the chapter. The pronoun may be translated “it,” referring to the silver rather than to Abraham, and the context favors that reading. The payment is a public gesture that “covers the eyes” of all who might whisper about Sarah’s time in the royal household; anyone who sees it will know that the king acknowledged a wrong and that her honor stands intact. To “all that are with thee, and with all other,” the matter is settled.

The closing clause, “thus she was reproved,” renders a verb that can mean to set right or decide a case. Many translations take it as “you are vindicated” or “you are cleared before everyone,” which fits the flow of the speech. Yet the KJV rendering also carries a truth. Sarah had shared in the deception, and the king’s words to her contain a measured reproof even as they restore her standing. God’s care for Sarah does not overlook her part in the scheme, and His mercy toward her does not wait for her to earn it.

wordNotes.term: כְּסוּת עֵינַיִם (kesut ʿenayim) — a covering of the eyes
wordNotes.explanation: כְּסוּת (kesut) is a covering or garment, used elsewhere of clothing and bedding. With “eyes,” the phrase is an idiom found only here, probably meaning something that causes observers to overlook or dismiss a suspected wrong. Here it most naturally describes the gift as public compensation that silences reproach and confirms Sarah’s innocence.

wordNotes.term: וְנֹכָחַת (wenokhaḥat) — thus she was reproved
wordNotes.explanation: The verb יָכַח (yakaḥ) means to decide, argue a case, or set right, and can include rebuke. In this passive form it most likely means Sarah is set right or vindicated. The related noun in Job describes an arbiter who could judge between two parties.

verses.bibleText: So Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So Abraham prayed unto God.” The sentence is brief, but it carries the turning point God had announced in verse 7. The man rebuked by Abimelech now does what only he could do, standing before God on behalf of the king who had been injured by his deceit. No record of his words is preserved. The narrator simply states that he prayed, and that God answered: “God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.”

This is the first time Scripture uses the verb “heal” with God as its subject. The word will later become a divine name in Israel’s experience: “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exodus 15:26). Healing here includes the restoration of the king himself, apparently from the illness that had kept him from Sarah, and the reopening of the wombs that had been closed, so that the royal household could again bear children. Life and fertility return through prayer, showing that God’s power over life operates in the courts of the nations as surely as in Abraham’s tent.

The prayer also reshapes Abraham. He had come to Gerar afraid for his own life; he leaves as the instrument through which God gives life to others. The pattern recurs in Scripture. Job prays for the friends who had misrepresented God, and the LORD restores Job when he prays (Job 42:8–10). Moses prays for Miriam after her rebellion (Numbers 12:13). Intercession is a ministry entrusted to those who have themselves needed mercy, and it does not wait for the intercessor to be flawless. “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16), James writes, citing Elijah, “a man subject to like passions as we are.”

The scene points forward to Christ, the true Intercessor for the nations. Abraham prayed for a household he had endangered; Christ intercedes for a world that endangered Him and crucified Him, praying even then, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). His intercession continues in the heavenly sanctuary, where He appears in the presence of God for us (Hebrews 9:24).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּרְפָּא אֱלֹהִים (wayyirpaʾ ʾelohim) — and God healed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb רָפָא (rapaʾ), to heal or restore, appears here for the first time in the Bible. Its range covers bodily healing, restored fruitfulness, and national renewal. The divine title in Exodus, “the LORD that healeth thee,” uses the same verb.

verses.bibleText: For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final verse looks back to explain what had been happening throughout Sarah’s stay: “For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham’s wife.” The duration implied is significant. Enough time had passed for the household to notice that no woman was conceiving, which means Sarah had been in Gerar long enough for the danger to be real and for God’s protection to be evident to all.

For the first time in the chapter the narrator uses the covenant name, the LORD. Throughout the episode God has dealt with Abimelech as Elohim, the Judge of all nations. Now, at the close, the narrative reveals that the One who closed the wombs was the LORD, the God of Abraham’s covenant, acting to protect the covenant marriage. The same verb, “restrained,” had come from Sarah’s lips years earlier when she said, “the LORD hath restrained me from bearing” (16:2). The irony is sharp. In Gerar, Sarah’s presence closes every womb in the royal house; when she leaves, those wombs open, while hers remains closed for one more chapter. But the LORD who closed and opened wombs in Gerar is about to open hers, and the next verse in Genesis will say, “The LORD visited Sarah as he had said” (21:1).

The chapter ends with the full title, “Sarah Abraham’s wife.” What the deception had obscured, the narrative states plainly. God guards what He has joined, and His promise stands secure.

wordNotes.term: עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה (ʿatsor ʿatsar YHWH) — the LORD had fast closed up
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive with the finite verb of עָצַר (ʿatsar), to restrain or shut up, intensifies the action: the closing was complete. Sarah used the same verb of her own barrenness. The appearance of the covenant name here shows that Abraham’s God was the One at work in Gerar.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why would a man who had just interceded boldly for Sodom fall back, in a quiet border town, into the same fear that had shamed him in Egypt?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: When God’s servant fails through fear and half-truth, God still guards His promise, defends the vulnerable, exposes the sin, and makes even the flawed believer a channel of blessing through intercession.
discussionQuestions: What does Abraham’s explanation in verses 11–13 reveal about how fear reshapes the way a believer reads other people and even his own calling?
How does God’s statement “I also withheld thee from sinning against me” shape our understanding of temptation and divine restraint?
Why must Abimelech still return Sarah and seek prayer even though God acknowledges his integrity?
What does the chapter teach about marriage and adultery long before the law was written at Sinai?
How can a believer who has been rightly rebuked still serve as an intercessor for others?
commonMisunderstandings: Abraham’s claim that Sarah was his half sister does not make his words honest; a statement framed to create a false impression is deception.
Abimelech’s integrity does not show that sincere outsiders are saved by their own goodness; God credits his clear conscience while still directing him to restitution and to the prophet’s prayer.
The chapter does not repeat chapter 12 by accident; the echo is deliberate and shows how an old weakness can return after years of faithfulness.
God’s protection of Abraham is not approval of his conduct; the same narrative that preserves him also lets a pagan king rebuke him.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the honesty of the narrative and the faithfulness of God together: Abraham’s fear is exposed without softening, and the promise survives only because God guards Sarah, restrains Abimelech, and keeps His word.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring your recurring fears into the light, refuse the half-truths that protect self at others’ expense, and trust the God who keeps His promises to make you a blessing even after you have failed.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s saving promise rests on His faithfulness and grace, not on the reliability of His servants, and He provides an Intercessor through whom guilty people may live.
flow: Even a man of great faith can fall into fear and deceit, and his sin harms others.
God sees the heart, restrains evil, and declares the penalty of sin to be death.
God provides a way of life through restitution and the prayer of His appointed intercessor.
Abraham’s imperfect intercession points to Christ, the sinless Intercessor who lives to plead for us.
Those who receive mercy are called to walk in truth and become channels of blessing.
simpleIllustrations: A guardrail on a mountain road does not praise the driver who drifts toward the edge; it simply keeps the car from going over. God’s restraint of Abimelech worked like that, holding back a wrong neither man fully saw.
A half-true answer is like a map with the river left off: every line on it may be accurate, yet anyone who trusts it will be led into danger.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the Intercessor God has provided, confess the fears and half-truths you have relied on, and let Him make your life a blessing to others?
cautions: Do not use Abraham’s failure to excuse deception or to suggest that God overlooks sin in His favored people.
Do not present Abimelech as saved by sincerity; keep the focus on God’s grace and the provision of intercession.
Handle Sarah’s vulnerability with care, and do not treat her as merely an object in the story.

reflectionQuestions: Where have I let an old fear return after I thought God had already taught me to trust Him?
Have I ever told a technically accurate story that I knew would leave a false impression?
How often do I assume there is “no fear of God” in people around me without truly knowing them?
Whom has my failure placed at risk, and what would honest restitution look like?
For whom should I be praying, even if I have personally been in the wrong toward them?
